text.title: Futures surge 1.4%-2.4% as AI-trade rebound hopes meet a shortened Black Friday session
text.summary: US futures point to a sharp rebound after a bruising month, with Nasdaq 100 futures up 2.4%, S&P 500 futures up 1.7% and Dow futures up 1.4%. Headlines frame it as a tech recovery gathering pace after weeks of AI anxiety. Asia led overseas (Hang Seng +3.3%, Nikkei +2.1%) and Europe followed more modestly. The VIX is easing but still elevated at 25.2. Oil, gold, the dollar and Bitcoin are all higher, so this is not a clean risk-on move across assets. The main thread is whether beaten-down tech can stabilize in a thin, holiday-shortened session.
text.rates: The 10-year Treasury yield closed Wednesday at 4.85%, down 5 bp, and is down 22 bp over five days. The 2-year is at 4.61%. Falling yields reduce the discount rate on future earnings, which typically helps richly valued growth stocks, consistent with the tech-led bounce. The headlines don't explain the bond rally. The dollar index is slightly higher at 103.84 (+0.2%). Gold jumped 3.7% to $3,697.5, and the headlines offer no explanation for the move.
text.breadth: Asia set a constructive tone: the Hang Seng gained 3.3% and the Nikkei 2.1%. Europe followed with smaller gains, and the VIX slipped to 25.2, down 5.9%, though it remains 43.9% above its level a month ago. Futures show the gains are broad: the Russell 2000 is up 1.5% and the Dow up 1.4%, not just tech. Thanksgiving week volumes are thin and Friday's session is shortened, so moves can overshoot in either direction.
text.context: The S&P 500 closed Wednesday at 7,182.78, down 6.4% over a month and 7.3% below its one-month high. The Nasdaq is 11.2% below its high. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap (data through Nov 20) notes a steep selloff in which technology and growth lagged value, and energy remained the leading S&P sector year to date. Today's futures gains would recoup only a part of the recent losses.
text.takeaway: Sharp drops and rebounds are a normal feature of markets, and corrections have not always led to bear markets or recessions. For diversified long-term investors, the sector and style dispersion this month is a reminder of why broad exposure matters.
text.talk: Futures are rallying this morning as investors look for a rebound in tech after a rough November, though the AI debate is unresolved and volatility remains elevated. Today's session is shortened, so moves may be exaggerated, and next week's jobs data is the next big test.

drivers.t: Bloomberg says US investors return from the holiday to a futures rally as a tech recovery gains momentum, and WSJ reports stocks poised to end the week strong as investors take a break from AI jitters. Nasdaq 100 futures are up 2.4%, the biggest move of the major gauges. Growth stocks are long-duration assets, so when worries about AI spending ease and yields drift lower, the most heavily sold names tend to bounce hardest. Dow futures are up about 600 points, putting the index on pace for its best week since April 2025, per CNBC.

drivers.h: Nvidia and AI sentiment remain fragile
drivers.t: MarketWatch notes Nvidia has dropped 27% over a chaotic month, with Jensen Huang facing congressional questions in the week ahead. Reuters Market Talk carries a view that Huang's return is a governance problem, and CNBC asks whether it can revive a shaky AI market. The FT describes a market struggling to price future earnings, with wild swings overshadowing the AI trade. Nvidia is a heavyweight in cap-weighted indexes, so its direction shapes the Nasdaq and S&P. Today's bounce may be sharp, but the debate over AI's durability is unresolved.

CNBC notes the November selloff has put the S&P 500 in a correction, and history shows corrections don't always become bear markets or recessions. MarketWatch adds that analysts raised profit forecasts for S&P 500 companies during the selloff. If earnings estimates rise while prices fall, valuations compress. That is the case dip-buyers make, though it does not guarantee a floor. Bloomberg says traders are arguing for a short-term rebound.

Europe is up (Euro Stoxx 50 +1.1%, DAX +0.7%, FTSE +0.6%) despite a soft backdrop. Reuters reports France is in a technical recession after revisions, and EU leaders cut budget talks short without agreeing a long-term funding plan. ECB Governing Council member Dolenc said the ECB's two rate hikes this year probably aren't enough to bring inflation back to 2%. Weak growth alongside a hawkish central bank is a tough mix for European equities. Spain's snap election on Sunday adds political uncertainty.

Rheinmetall said it will take a more prudent approach to forecasting sales of tanks and ammunition as Europe's rearmament boom hits hurdles, a reminder that even strong themes face execution limits. SAP is reportedly weighing at least 10,000 job cuts as it reshapes its software business around AI. That shows how AI is changing cost structures, not just creating demand. Together they show AI and defense spending are being repriced for realism, not just enthusiasm.

drivers.h: Oil firmer on Gulf supply worries
drivers.t: WTI is up 1.6% to $85.02, its third straight gain. Reuters reports oil gains lifted UAE stocks amid Gulf supply disruption fears. Higher crude can feed inflation expectations and squeeze consumers, but it supports energy producers. WTI is still 16.5% below its one-month high, so today's move is a modest bounce within a bigger pullback.

watch.why: WSJ says labor data will shape expectations ahead of the Fed's December rate decision, which drives yields and equity valuations.
Nvidia's 27% monthly drop makes any news from the hearings a potential swing factor for AI-linked stocks.
The outcome could shift Spain's political direction and add to European uncertainty alongside the failed EU budget talks.
Thin volume after the holiday can exaggerate moves in either direction, including today's futures rally.
